Following arrows, only the cycle and the two-way pair are mutually reachable, so there are four strong components, A, B, C in the accent color, D, E in teal, and the singletons F in violet and G in gold, listed on the card in the same colors." width="100%"} For directed graphs, a strongly connected component (SCC) is a maximal set of nodes where every node is reachable from every other node following directed edges. Uses Kosaraju's algorithm for efficient computation. For undirected graphs, returns the same result as `weakly_connected_components()` since strong connectivity equals regular connectivity when edges are bidirectional. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[set[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of sets, where each set contains the node IDs in a strongly connected component. Components are returned in no particular order. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Kosaraju's algorithm (1978) computes SCCs in $O(V + E)$ time with three passes: first a DFS on the original graph produces a finish-time ordering, then the edge set is reversed, and a second DFS on the reversed graph in reverse-finish order carves out one SCC per tree it produces. The correctness argument is elegant: a node's SCC is exactly the set of vertices reachable from it in both $G$ and its transpose $G^\top$. Tarjan's algorithm delivers the same guarantee in a single DFS pass with an explicit stack; both are common choices, and any downstream code should treat the returned component list as unordered. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Nodes `A`, `B`, and `C` form a cycle, so each can reach the others and they collapse into one strongly connected component; `D` is reachable from the cycle but has no way back, so it forms its own component: ::: {#fa518c11 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), # Creates a cycle -> SCC {A, B, C} ("C", "D"), # D is reachable but can't reach back ] ) ) sccs = graph.strongly_connected_components() # Returns 2: {A, B, C} and {D} len(sccs) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: In a web graph, SCCs represent "communities" of mutually linked pages; finding the largest one highlights the biggest tightly-linked cluster: ::: {#69c1fd3a .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), # SCC of 3 ("C", "D"), # D is a separate SCC ] ) ) sccs = graph.strongly_connected_components() largest_scc = max(sccs, key=len) # Returns 3 (A, B, C form the largest cluster) len(largest_scc) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 3 ``` ::: :::
